newsitem.title: POLAND: INTERVIEW - Biggest Polish beer holding eyes growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Biggest Polish beer holding eyes growth.

text.p: The two Polish brewers in which South African Breweries Ltd (SAB) has a strategic stake, Lech and Tychy, plan to continue high investment and lift market share by 10 to 15 percent by the decade's end.
The two breweries currently command more than 20 percent of Poland's burgeoning beer market.

Lech board chairman Jan Kulczyk told Reuters late on Thursday that his agricultural holding Euro Agro Centrum SA and SAB would invest its pledged $115 million in Tychy in three to four years rather than over the originally stated five.
"We're going to do it (invest) quicker...it could be done over three years, though we aren't able to invest too fast since the very technological process needs time," Kulczyk said.

In late September a joint venture of Euro Agro Centrum and SAB paid the state treasury $75 million for a 52-percent stake in Tychy. Earlier SAB had acquired a 25-percent stake in Lech through its investment in one of Kulczyk's companies.

Lech and Tychy, according to Piwochmiel beer research firm, upped sales by 24.6 percent and 15.8 percent respectively over 1996's first three quarters, the most dynamic growth among Poland's top-five brewers, which produce about 60 percent of the country's beer.

Kulczyk, soon to become Tychy's board chairman as well, said investment at Tychy would help lift the firm's annual production to three million hectolitres annually from the current 1.5 million hectolitres by 1999 or 2000.
He said Lech's sales-growth dynamic could reach 38 percent over the next few years.

He also said Lech, whose full name is Lech Browary Wielkopolski SA, would continue to receive "a lot" of investment after Euro Agro Centrum injected $75 million during the past three years, though he would not say how much.

Over 1996's first three quarters Lech trailed two other all-Poland vendors, Elbrewery Company Ltd (EB) and Zaklady Piwowarskie w Zywcu SA (Zywiec) in market share, but led Okocimskie Zaklady Piwowarskie SA (Okocim).
Tychy, whose full name is Browary Tyskie Gorny Slask SA, concentrates largely in the southern Polish region of Upper Silesia, where it commands a 75-percent market share.
"It's a Silesian regional brewer, we don't have any definite plans to expand to all of Poland," Kulczyk said.

Sales in Upper Silesia, where per-capita annual beer consumption is estimated closer to the 100-plus litres of several Western European countries, have helped Tychy trail only EB in national market share.
Outside of Upper Silesia the average Pole drinks 37 litres of beer annually, Salomon Brothers said in a recent report.
In the first three quarters of 1996 Polish brewers sold almost 13 million hectolitres of beer, up 8.2 percent over the same period of last year.
The number is seen rising as the country's middle class grows in relation to the traditional vodka-drinking population.
Kulczyk said SAB's help in cutting costs especially in distribution and accounting would also help lift profits, which would continue to be invested.
"They have experience in a lot of different countries and they adapt to local conditions, which for example look different in China than in South Africa," Kulczyk said.
SAB, which in the region also has three breweries in Romania and two in Hungary, also has three breweries in China in addition to breweries in South Africa.
Kulczyk said the holding had no plans to buy another Polish brewer or list shares on the Warsaw Stock Exchange.
